The practice is known as plunderphonics. Similar to making a collage, artists take samples from other recorded works and then arrange and manipulate them into original works of art. An early example would be the Residents' single "Beyond the Valley of a Day in the Life," which samples the Beatles. The Avalanches are the one of the most acclaimed plunderers in contemporary music. Their new album Wildflower has been getting a lot of buzz in audiophile circles as a potential album of the year.

Plunderphonics artists justify their work by stating that they create completely new compositions from the samples. After all, every artist borrows from artists before them. "Good artists imitate, great artists steal," as the saying goes.

So here's my question: should copyright law favor protecting intellectual property, or does that hinder creativity? Should we favor the right of individuals to maintain the integrity of what they've created or instead encourage individuals to reimagine old works into new? Where can the balance be struck?
What do you think about musicians making original compositions from pirated content, and potentially profiting from it? Is it right?

The term plunderphonics has a very broad definition and therefore is impossible to say if I agree or disagree with it.

In cases like Vanilla Ice sampling and slightly altering the bass line of Under Pressure I would argue that there is clear violation of ones copyright. Hell, one only needs to listen to the opening and they will be confused as to which song it is until the rest of the song comes in.

However, in cases like RaggaJungle where an entire genre revolves around the deconstruction and reassembling of the Amen Break and where truly unique pieces are created I can only look at that as a building on top of ones copyrights and truly artistic avenues of expression can be achieved.

A better example of this is explained in the Amen Break video.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5SaFTm2bcac

Yeah, I was pretty much asking where to draw the line. But, we love in a strange time. Before modern popular music, no one thought to copyright folk and blues standards. It was pretty much expected that musicians would sample or completely rip off songwriters, alter the lyrics or chord progression slightly, and call it their own. Now, doing that would get you in big trouble.

Do you think Quuen or David Bowie suffered financially from Vanilla Ice's use of the bass line?

Do you think Quuen or David Bowtie suffered financially from Vanilla Ice's use of the bass line?

No because Vanilla Ice did pay them. ;)

When it comes to music, unless they are supporters of Creative Commons I have mixed feelings about it.

To explain a bit more. Is the sample creating a new and different song? Yes. Does that mean the original artist shouldn't get paid? No. But, must they get paid? No. At the very least, proper attribution should be made. Unless the new artist has some kind of confirmation from the original artist that they can use their work (or, in the case of Trent Resnor, all samples being made freely available and encouraged to remix) then it would be best to not use that sample and find something else if you really must use a sample instead of make your own.

It's a weird situation my thoughts are with copyright laws. But, I do think that they are too strict, especially with the Sonny Bono Act.

I tend to agree. The thing that makes copyright law so restrictive is the length of time that needs to pass before a work goes into the public domain. I think Richard Stallman suggested to reduce it to 7 years. It would be an interesting experiment. It's at 70 now, iirc.
I have no problems if it was for the life of the creator.
Fair use doctrine covers sampling. As long as you don't reproduce a substantial part of the original work, it's totally legit.
Part of the problem there is that the lawyers are busy trying to destroy any practical ability to apply fair use, unfortunately.

I love plunderphonics, but the artists should make sure to get all their samples cleared if they're going to sell their work for a profit. Other people created the music they're using, and it's only fair to get permission from them first.

Not an unreasonable position, however, the counterargument is pretty convincing to me. Similar to @0x4F's argument.

To plunderphonics artists, samples are intruments. Given the fact that I'm a libertarian leftist who questions of intellectual property is even a useful concept, I don't really see how, at least in theory, artists should be required to pay to use data that they already presumably purchased. It's like buying a guitar and then having to pay the guitar company every time you decide to make money with it.
